lesson.name: Sharded matrix multiplication and result ownership
lesson.role: Derive the communication operation from the partitioned matrix axis and the next consumer’s required result layout.
lesson.description: A compiler must preserve both a tensor’s values and who owns them. Splitting matrix output rows gives different ranks independent output rows; splitting the contracted inner dimension gives each rank only part of every output sum. Those are different meanings of a local matrix product, even if the local arrays have similar shapes. JAX’s explicit sharding example forms local products and then reduces their partial sums. A sum all-reduce makes the completed result available at every rank. Reduce-scatter instead finishes the sum while distributing different output pieces, and all-gather can later assemble those pieces when a consumer needs a replica. Concatenating unfinished partial sums does not perform their missing arithmetic. This distinction connects tensor-axis information in a compiler to the collective scheduled over the network. It also prevents allocating replicas merely because the preceding stage happened to use all-reduce. A valid next operator may consume distributed rows directly, while another needs a different layout and an explicit conversion. The example below uses exactly representable small integers; its equality does not imply arbitrary floating-point reduction trees are bitwise identical.
mechanism: Declare C = AB, the complete tensor shapes, stored element size and required consumer ownership before partitioning.
Split the inner dimension into disjoint sets Kᵣ; each rank receives matching columns of A and rows of B.
Compute Cᵣ locally. Each Cᵣ covers all output coordinates but contains only the products indexed by Kᵣ.
Add contributions with matching output coordinates. Use all-reduce for replicated C or reduce-scatter for completed disjoint output shards.
Retain row shards when the next operation can use them; all-gather only when the consumer requires the whole tensor.
Check every output against a separate dense reference, and count a sent payload once at its chosen link boundary. Input distribution, temporary buffers and protocol overhead are additional costs.

science.title: Two-rank payload ledger
science.equation: Qreduce-scatter = 8 bytes/rank; Qall-gather = 8 bytes/rank; Qcombined = 16 bytes/rank
science.explanation: For this explicitly described two-rank, 2×2 float32-output schedule, each phase sends one two-element row per rank.
science.assumptions: Logical payload sent by each rank in this chosen exchange; excludes initial input placement, headers, retransmission, local reads/writes and actual collective implementation details.

lesson.engineeringExample: Use A = [[1,2],[3,4]] and B = [[5,6],[7,8]]. Rank 0 owns k=0 and forms C₀ = [[5,6],[15,18]]; rank 1 owns k=1 and forms C₁ = [[14,16],[28,32]]. Reduce-scatter with row ownership sends C₀ row 1 [15,18] from rank 0 to rank 1, and C₁ row 0 [14,16] in the opposite direction. Rank 0 adds [5,6]+[14,16]=[19,22]; rank 1 adds [15,18]+[28,32]=[43,50]. Each sends 8 payload bytes if elements are float32. If both consumers need all of C, all-gather exchanges these completed rows for another 8 bytes sent per rank. Both then hold [[19,22],[43,50]]. Total sent payload is 16 bytes per rank, 32 across the two senders; counting the matching receives again would double-count this network boundary. Concatenating the two original 2×2 partial matrices would create four rows and would leave their sums unfinished.
lesson.learningObjective: Reconstruct the same 2×2 product from inner-dimension shards, choose a collective from output ownership, and reconcile the two-rank payload ledger.
lesson.misconception: A shard can be an unfinished contribution to every output, not necessarily a disjoint piece of the finished output.

lesson.name: Uneven batches and the global gradient
lesson.role: Preserve the intended training objective when ranks contribute different numbers of valid examples or tokens.
lesson.description: A synchronized gradient can be consistent across replicas and still represent the wrong objective. Suppose the intended loss is the mean over all valid training items in one optimizer update. A rank that averages two items and a rank that averages six have already divided by different denominators. Averaging their two gradient means assigns the smaller batch more influence per item. The global item mean instead weights each local mean by its valid-item count. PyTorch’s pinned DistributedDataParallel contract documents averaging gradients between workers, so the loss normalization and collective normalization must be considered together. The count can mean examples, unmasked target tokens or a sum of explicit sample weights; choosing it is part of the objective, not a hardware detail. This lesson derives one scalar update from a concrete squared-error loss. It assumes the same current parameter at both ranks and no cross-sample operation such as batch-dependent normalization. A rank exhausting its entire input stream is a separate synchronization problem: matching collective participation does not by itself fix per-item weighting.
mechanism: Define which items count in the loss and record their global count N for this optimizer update. Exclude padding only when the objective says to exclude it.
Compute local loss sums or local means and retain the valid count associated with each reduction.
For a rank-mean reducer over P active participants, scale a local mean gradient by P nᵣ/N before the averaging collective. Equivalently reduce local sums and divide once by N.
During gradient accumulation, use the count over the entire update window rather than silently averaging unequal microbatch means.
Apply the same synchronized gradient and optimizer state transition at every replica, then compare the result with the unpartitioned reference objective.
Handle empty local contributions and exhausted ranks with explicit participation rules; never divide an empty local mean by zero or simply omit a required collective.

science.title: Global item-mean gradient
science.equation: N = Σr nᵣ; g = (1/N) Σr nᵣ ḡᵣ
science.explanation: Each local ḡᵣ is the mean of gradients for nᵣ valid equally weighted items. Multiply by nᵣ to recover the local sum.
science.assumptions: N>0, same parameters and differentiable separable per-item loss. No cross-sample dependence; sample weights replace counts when the objective uses unequal weights.

science.title: Compensate a mean-across-ranks reducer
science.equation: g = (1/P) Σr [(P nᵣ/N) ḡᵣ]; wnew = w − ηg
science.explanation: The factor P nᵣ/N ensures the subsequent division by P leaves the intended global item mean.
science.assumptions: P fixed participating ranks for this update; no custom reducer scaling. The scalar SGD update has no momentum, clipping, weight decay or loss scaling.

lesson.engineeringExample: Take ℓ(w;y)=½(w−y)² at w=10. Rank 0 has targets [9,9], producing gradients [1,1], count 2 and mean 1. Rank 1 has [7,7,7,7,7,7], producing six gradients of 3, count 6 and mean 3. The unpartitioned objective has gradient (2×1+6×3)/8=2.5. Averaging rank means gives (1+3)/2=2 instead. With learning rate 0.1, correct SGD gives wnew=9.75; the unweighted rank mean gives 9.8. For a reducer that divides by P=2, scale the local means by 2×2/8=0.5 and 2×6/8=1.5. It then averages 0.5 and 4.5 to obtain 2.5. If the ranks each held four valid items, equal weighting would be appropriate. Token-level training needs the valid target-token count when that is the declared loss denominator; sequence counts need not be proportional.
lesson.learningObjective: Derive and test a globally normalized gradient from unequal local batch means, then distinguish objective equivalence from replica synchronization.
lesson.misconception: A mean across ranks is a mean across training items only when local denominators and weights make it so.

lesson.name: Floating-point reductions and compiler permissions
lesson.shortName: The order of a floating-point sum
lesson.role: Distinguish algebraic equivalence, numerical error and bitwise reproducibility when compilation or collectives regroup arithmetic.
lesson.description: Real-number addition is associative, but a floating-point implementation rounds intermediate results. Changing the reduction tree changes where those rounding steps occur. A compiler that vectorizes a sum or a distributed library that groups rank contributions differently can therefore produce different low bits, and cancellation can make the difference much larger relative to the final result. LLVM exposes reassociation as an explicit fast-math permission; permission to contract a multiply and add is a separate choice. Such options should be read as part of the numerical contract, not assumed to be enabled in every program. A fixed reduction schedule can improve repeatability without establishing that its answer is the most accurate. Conversely, a numerically acceptable answer need not be bitwise identical to another legal result. The small integer schedules elsewhere in the atlas deliberately avoid this issue by keeping every operation exactly representable. This lesson changes that arithmetic assumption while keeping the underlying sum visible.
mechanism: Specify input representation, accumulator dtype, rounding mode and treatment of fused operations before comparing outputs.
Write out the intermediate additions imposed by the chosen serial, vector or distributed reduction order.
Round after each stated operation rather than rounding only the final real-number sum.
Inspect compiler reassociation and contraction permissions, plus the library and rank topology that determine the actual reduction tree.
Compare with an independent higher-precision or exact reference where available; use an absolute tolerance near cancellation and a justified relative tolerance elsewhere.
Validate downstream loss or task behavior separately. A repeatability check and a numerical-accuracy check answer different questions.

science.title: Spacing at the chosen magnitude
science.explanation: In the binary32 interval [2²⁴,2²⁵), adjacent representable values are two apart. The halfway sum 2²⁴+1 rounds to the even lower significand.
science.assumptions: ULP here means the spacing immediately above 2²⁴. Spacing immediately below that power of two is 1; it is not constant across the boundary.

lesson.engineeringExample: Let a=16,777,216=2²⁴, b=1 and c=−16,777,216, all representable in binary32. Group left: a+b is exactly 16,777,217 before rounding, halfway between representable 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Ties-to-even gives 16,777,216; adding c then gives 0. Group right: b+c=−16,777,215 is representable, so adding a gives 1. The exact mathematical sum is 1. A deterministic left reduction repeats 0 and is reproducible, yet its absolute error is 1. A hypothetical acceptance condition |computed−reference|≤0.01 rejects 0 and accepts 1. That tolerance is an authored condition for this example, not an accuracy threshold for real training. Accumulating these three binary32 inputs with sufficiently precise binary64 additions produces 1; this does not guarantee that wider accumulation always eliminates error in larger problems.
lesson.learningObjective: Reproduce both binary32 reduction orders and explain why compiler permissions, accuracy checks and reproducibility requirements must be specified separately.
lesson.misconception: Bitwise repeatability does not prove closeness to the exact result, and algebraic equivalence does not prove bitwise identity.

lesson.name: Speculative decoding: proposals and verified output
lesson.role: Account for target-distributed output tokens while separating draft work, verification and actual elapsed time.
lesson.description: A draft model can propose several next tokens cheaply, but proposals are not yet accepted output. In strict speculative sampling, the target model evaluates the relevant conditional distributions and verifies the draft sequence in order. A proposal is accepted with a probability determined by the target-to-draft probability ratio. The first rejected position is corrected using the positive residual between the two distributions, and later proposals from that speculative branch are discarded. When all proposals are accepted, one additional target token can be emitted. This procedure preserves the target sampling distribution under its stated assumptions; it does not establish factual truth or force the same sampled text from the same random seed. The benefit can come from evaluating several target positions together and reusing data movement, while draft work, rejected work and additional state still consume resources. The exact three-symbol example below checks the sampling correction before considering a separately assumed timing budget.
mechanism: Use target p and draft q distributions over the same token events and the same valid prefix, including any declared sampling transforms.
Sample a proposal x from q; when q(x)>0, accept it with probability min(1,p(x)/q(x)). A symbol with q(x)=0 cannot be proposed.
After the first rejection, sample a correction from normalized max(p−q,0) at that prefix and discard the later speculative branch.
If all γ proposals are accepted, draw the extra token from the target distribution conditioned on the full accepted prefix.
Count accepted prefix tokens plus the one correction or bonus token as output; count draft proposals and rejected target work separately.

Measure draft, target-verification, synchronization and state-management time on the actual workload before claiming a speedup. Distributional equivalence remains separate from factual or task correctness.

science.title: Acceptance and rejection correction
science.explanation: For a proposed symbol, accept with a(x). After a rejection, sample from residual r. Total acceptance probability is α=Σx min(p(x),q(x)).
science.assumptions: Finite normalized distributions with q(x)>0 for a proposed x. Use r only when its denominator is positive; if p=q no rejection occurs. Exact probability arithmetic and consistent prefixes are assumed.

science.title: Output count in the iid acceptance scenario
science.equation: E[K] = Σj=0…γ αʲ; Rscenario = E[K]/(Tdraft + Tverify + Toverhead)
science.explanation: K counts output tokens, including the correction or bonus. With iid acceptance probability α and no early stopping, the probability of accepting at least j proposals is αʲ.
science.assumptions: The iid assumption is synthetic; actual acceptance varies with prefix. Time terms are separately declared seconds per verification round; no measured speedup, energy reduction or universal latency scaling is implied.

lesson.engineeringExample: For symbols A/B/C, choose target p=[0.6,0.3,0.1] and draft q=[0.2,0.3,0.5]. Conditional acceptance is [1,1,0.2], so accepted probability mass is [0.2,0.3,0.1] and total α=0.6. The rejected mass is 0.4; normalized positive residual p−q is [1,0,0], so every correction in this toy case is A. The final output distribution is [0.2,0.3,0.1]+0.4×[1,0,0]=[0.6,0.3,0.1], exactly the target distribution. If γ=2 and acceptance events are independently 0.6 at both positions, output counts 1,2,3 have probabilities 0.4,0.24,0.36. Thus E[K]=1.96 tokens. Separately assume the two draft steps together take 2 ms, target verification 6 ms and overhead 1 ms: 1.96/0.009≈217.8 output tokens/s. A 6 ms single-token baseline would be 166.7 tokens/s under those assumptions. At 12 ms verification, the speculative scenario instead gives 130.7 tokens/s. Neither timing is measured or taken from the paper; acceptance alone does not establish acceleration.
lesson.learningObjective: Recover the target distribution by exact probability accounting, then calculate output-per-round and a conditional throughput without treating proposals or assumptions as measured useful output.
lesson.misconception: Accepting a draft token validates it against a sampling distribution, not against external facts; higher acceptance does not by itself prove lower latency.

check.question: In the stated toy distributions, a rejected proposal must be corrected from which distribution?
check.explanation: The positive residual is [0.4,0,0], which normalizes to [1,0,0]. Adding its weighted contribution recovers the target probabilities.

checks.question: Under iid α=0.6 with two proposals, what is the expected output count including correction or bonus?
Does preserving p establish that sampled statements are true?
checks.explanation: The target distribution can assign probability to factually wrong continuations.

lesson.whyAI: Useful serving throughput counts the output that survives the verification algorithm and meets the task’s quality requirements. This connects decoding semantics, memory reuse and latency accounting.
lesson.tradeoff: More proposals can expose useful parallel verification while increasing draft computation, temporary state and wasted work. Prefix-dependent acceptance and workload-specific target cost determine the result.
lesson.evidenceNotes: The cited ICML paper establishes the strict correction algorithm and the explicitly iid output-count formula. The toy probabilities, output-count distribution and all millisecond values are authored. No private model, serving implementation, benchmark speedup or quality improvement is asserted.

equations.text: Accept a proposed symbol using the target-to-draft ratio capped at one. After rejection, sample from the normalized positive target-minus-draft residual. Acceptance mass sums the minimum of each pair of probabilities.

claims.statement: The cited speculative-decoding algorithm uses acceptance and residual sampling to retain the target sampling distribution.
